title: Model fallback & resilience — hyperscaler warroom notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick, tactical brief for GTM (AE + SE + CS) on how to position Redwood vs hyperscaler managed endpoints when the buyer’s main concern is reliability, graceful degradation, and model-level control. This is a working note — expect edits and additions.

Thesis (one-liner):
Hyperscalers sell managed endpoints as convenience; Redwood wins where predictability, controlled degradation (fallbacks), and model-serving operational primitives matter to product SLAs and unit economics.

Primary buyer signal:
- Customer has production LLM features with SLOs (p95 latency, availability), and worried about tail latency, noisy multi-tenant neighbors, or regulatory controls (data locality).

High-level win themes (short):
- Deterministic fallbacks: model variants by latency/cost/SLA with automatic graceful degradation.
- Transparent unit economics: token-level + route-level cost visibility, predictable reserved capacity.
- Operational primitives: prefix/KV caching, warm pools, canary rollouts and rollback hooks, per-token tracing.
- Private parity: same APIs across hosted/dedicated/private; you don’t re-architect to move off Redwood.

What hyperscalers will claim (expected):
1) "We have managed endpoints and autoscaling — costs are lower at scale."
2) "We provide global infra and security — easier for enterprises."
3) "Tight cloud integration — cheaper egress and unified billing."
4) "We can host any model you want, bring your own model (BYOM)."

Concise rebuttals (soundbites for AE/SE):
1) Autoscaling != predictability. The autoscaler hides cold-start spikes and queueing costs — you get variable tail latency and unexpected regression windows. We provide warm pools + dedicated capacity + fallback chains so your p95 stays within SLO even during traffic surges.
2) Security is table stakes. Redwood’s Private offering includes customer control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit trails packaged for regulated industries — plus the same rollout and observability primitives your engineers rely on.
3) Unified billing is convenient but opaque. Our per-route, per-model cost breakdowns let you optimize prompts and select quantized variants with measurable ROI (we can show a simulated cost delta on a sample workload).
4) BYOM is useful, but hyperscalers lack inference-first runtime optimizations (KV/prefix caching, quantization-aware kernels, continuous batching). That’s where we squeeze real latency/cost wins.

Operational differentiators (talking points for SEs):
- Model fallback graph: show how a single request can failover to a cheaper/faster variant without failing the user experience. Demonstrate policy: latency-first vs cost-first.
- Prefix/KV caching: explain savings for chat/history-heavy flows (show sample numbers for 8-turn chat).
- Deterministic warm pools: how we precreate KV caches and maintain hot cores for stable p95.
- Traceability: token-level timing and error traces to tie regressions to PRs, config changes, or model swaps.
- Rollouts: canary by user-segment, automatic rollback on quality regressions (tied to evals).

Demo checklist (SE):
- Live failover demo: simulate primary variant OOM/latency and route traffic to fallback (5–10 minute setup).
- Cost transparency screen: show per-route token cost and a simple cost-savings scenario when enabling caching + quantized variant.
- Private vs Dedicated slide: highlight compliance support + same UX across modes.
- Quick trace: follow a token through batching -> kernel selection -> return.

Common buyer objections + scripts:
- "We already use managed endpoints in our cloud." -> "Great — where does that flow hit tail latency or unpredictable cost? We’ll run a 48h comparative trace on your workload to show real p95 and cost delta; if you don’t see advantage we’ll document the findings and move on."
- "Hyperscaler has broader ML platform integrations." -> "We integrate with their storage/identity where it helps, but we remove the guesswork for inference — let us be your predictable inference plane while you keep platform tools for training."
- "We can build similar runtime ourselves." -> "Teams underestimate the ops and steady-state costs: kernel tuning, caching strategy, rollout automation, and per-token telemetry. We can prove the break-even with a short POC (typically months of engineering saved)."

Pricing and economics message:
- Emphasize transparency: per-route breakdown, precommit options (Dedicated) to flatten unit cost, and Optimize tools to recommend quantization/batching with projected savings.
- Talk in sample workloads: show a 100k daily chat messages example and contrast total cost and p95 across three policies (low-latency, balanced, cost-first).

Competitive matrix (quick):
- Hyperscaler managed endpoints: broad infra, OK for non-latency-critical workloads, opaque cost, limited inference-specific optimizations.
- Redwood Hosted: fastest path for product teams needing predictable latency and cost transparency.
- Redwood Dedicated: for teams that need reserved throughput and isolated tenancy while keeping Redwood operational primitives.
- Redwood Private: enterprises needing VPC/on-prem + audit/KMS + same UX.

Battle tactics (field plays):
- If buyer is infra-led: emphasize operational primitives and SRE-friendly tooling (tracing, rollouts, fallbacks).
- If buyer is cost-led: run Optimize mini-POC and share concrete per-token savings and model suggestions.
- If buyer is compliance/security-led: show Private deployment checklist and SOC/ISO artifacts + KMS integration notes.

FAQ / quick facts (for AE cheat sheet):
- Q: "How do fallbacks affect output quality?" A: Policy defines tradeoffs; fallback variants can be prompt-engineered to preserve core semantics. We integrate evals to detect regressions and auto-rollback.
- Q: "Do fallbacks increase cost?" A: Not if configured proactively — we route by latency/cost budget and cache aggressively to avoid re-generation.
- Q: "How much dev work to migrate?" A: API-compatible routes + import tools; many customers onboard in < 6 weeks for core paths.

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Quantify fallback latencies/cost on sample customer workloads — ask Benchmarking team for 3 representative traces (chat, summarization, search-rewrite). (Owner: Marco)
- Create 1-pager for exec-level comparisons that contrasts SLA outcomes (p95/p99) not just price. (Owner: Sofia)
- Draft a 5-minute demo script for AE showing live canary rollback. (Owner: Devon)

Appendix — suggested collateral to attach to pitch: 
- Short case study: how fallback reduced user-facing errors in a fintech chat product (anonymized metrics).
- One-slide comparison of observability signals available (token timing, KV hits, model-version trace).
- Quick whitepaper: "Designing graceful degradation for LLM UX" (4–6 pages).

Notes to self:
- Keep this doc terse — field teams want snippets, not treatises.
- Follow up with Pricing to get sample calc templates for the demo.

End of notes.
